There's the solution in the following website:
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1q72AafnF6OLP71U2c0YcD1OTv1JHeB9s

De fato é um problema muito bacana. Acho que é natural pensar no TCR ao olhar pra um problema assim, daí a gente vai olhar pro caso  $m=p$  e resolver do jeito usual, por PCP mesmo. A questão é que o lema de Hensel é algo que eu particularmente não conhecia até ver esse problema, então na hora da prova eu me ferraria legal kkkkk. Talvez fosse natural acabar(sem querer) provando a versão fraca do lema, que foi o que consegui fazer, mas a versão forte(a qual resolve o caso  $p=2$ ), já não sei tanto...
Mas enfim, vou anotar aqui o pouco do que fiz tanto por fins de armazenamento, quanto pra deixar registrada nesse tópico a prova da versão fraca do lema. (Estou desconsiderando os casos de exceções, uma vez que são bem chatos e confesso que acho que não resolveria o  $p=2$ )

Queremos provar que sempre existem  $(x_k,y_k)$  tais que   $$ x_k^2+5y_k^2+2024\equiv 0(\text{mod}\ p´^k) $$   Porém, seria muito interessante se pudéssemos fixar  $y_k$  de modo a trabalharmos apenas com um polinômio de grau  $2$  em  $\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}[x]$ . 

Para ter uma ideia, vamos provar que  $m=p^2$  tem solução: Quero mostrar que existem  $(x_2,y_2)$  tal que  $x_2^2+5y_2^2+2024\equiv 0(\text{mod} \ p^2)$ .O que eu faria portanto, seria tomar  $y_2=y_1$  onde  $y_1$  é solução em  $\text{mod} \ p$  e olhar para o polinômio  $f(x)=x^2+5y_1^2+2024$ . Bom, eu sei que para um polinômio em  $\mathbb{Z}_n[x]$ , é uma boa olhar para a expansão  $f(x)= f(a) + f^,(a)(x-a) + \frac{2}{2!} f^{,,}(a)(x-a)^2$ , pois tenho mais liberdade de tomar um  $a$  esperto de tal modo que seja possível construir uma solução para  $f$  em  $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}[x]$ . No entanto, sei que devo, em algum momento utilizar a hipótese, então testemos  $a=x_1$ :   $$ f(x)= f(x_1) + f^,(x_1)(x-x_1) + f^{,,}(x_1)(x-x_1)^2\equiv 0 (\text{mod} \ p^2) $$     $$ \iff f(x_1) \equiv -f^,(x_1)(x-x_1)-f^{,,}(x_1)(x-x_1)^2(\text{mod} \ p^2) $$   Só que sei que  $f(x_1)$  é divisível por  $p$ , então seria muito interessante se conseguisse transformar essa equação  $\text{mod} \ p^2$  numa equação apenas  $\text{mod} \ p$ , uma vez que sei que sempre há solução. Logo, tome  $x=pm+x_1$  e veja que a congruência acima será equivalente a   $$ f(x_1) \equiv -f^,(x_1)pm-f^{,,}(x_1)p^2m^2 \equiv -f(x_1)pm (\text{mod} \ p^2) $$   nos dando o que queríamos! Então, vamos dividir tudo por  $p$  obtendo a equação   $$ \frac{f(x_1)}{p}\equiv -f^,(x_1)m(\text{mod} \ p) $$   Agora veja que tal  $m$  existe pois, se  $f^,(x_1)\equiv 0(\text{mod} \ p)$  significa que  $\frac{f(x_1)}{p}\equiv 0(\text{mod} \ p)$  logo temos automaticamente  $x_1$  como solução para  $\text{mod} \ p^2$ . Então, se nenhum dos dois é múltiplo de  $p$ , significa que  $m\equiv \frac{f(x_1)}{p}(-f^,(x_1))^{-1} (\text{mod} p)$  é tal que  $f(x_1+pm)\equiv 0(\text{mod}\ p^2)$ Bom, com isso, já temos uma ideia de como induzir e provar que para todos os primos que não dividem  $2024$  e que não são  $5$ ,  $m=p^k$  é solução. Os casos  $p=23$ ,  $5$  e  $11$  são até fazíveis utilizando essa ideia, mas um pouco modificada. Para o caso  $p=2$  de fato precisaríamos de uma abordagem mais detalhada que usa o lema de Hensel forte(o qual ainda não sei provar kk)

stem_md: In the cartesian plane, consider the subset of all the points with both integer coordinates. Prove that it is possible to choose a finite non-empty subset  $S$  of these points in such a way that any line  $l$  that forms an angle of  $90^{\circ},0^{\circ},135^{\circ}$  or  $45^{\circ}$  with the positive horizontal semi-axis intersects  $S$  at exactly  $2024$  points or at no points.
solution_md: Start with  $2024$  points in a line call it  $S_1$ . Then, replicate this set  $2024$  times vertically, with the points so far apart that no  $45^\circ$  or  $135^\circ$  line intersects this set, called  $S_2$ , more than once. Again, repeat this structure  $2024$  times diagonally making an angle of  $45^\circ$ , obtaining  $S_3$ . Finally, replicate this  $2024$  times diagonally, with an angle  $135^\circ$ , producing  $S_4$ . You will find that  $S_4$  meets the desired properties, as we can make the repetitions so far apart that each construction doesn’t interfere with the other properties.

stem_md: For each natural number  $n\ge3$ , let  $m(n)$  be the maximum number of points inside or on the sides of a regular  $n$ -agon of side  $1$  such that the distance between any two points is greater than  $1$ . Prove that  $m(n)\ge n$  for  $n>6$ .
solution_md: Let’s construct an example with  $m(n)=n$ . Place  $n-1$  points on the vertices of the  $n$ -agon and another at its centre. Then, dislocate the  $i$ -th point by  $\sec^i\theta\varepsilon\ll1$  clockwise along the edge, where  $\theta=\frac{2\pi}{n}$ . For  $n>6$ , we need not worry about the distances to points other than its neighbors or the centre. The former becomes  $d^2=(1-\varepsilon\sec^i\theta)^2+(\varepsilon\sec^{i+1}\theta)^2+2\varepsilon\sec^{i+1}\theta(1-\varepsilon\sec^i\theta)\cos\theta=$  $1+\varepsilon(-2\sec^i\theta+2\sec^i\theta)+\varepsilon^2(\sec^{2i}\theta+\sec^{2i+2}\theta-2\sec^{2i}\theta)=1+\varepsilon^2\sec^{2i}\theta\tan^2\theta>1$

stem_md: For a pair of integers  $a$  and  $b$ , with  $0<a<b<1000$ , a set  $S\subset \begin{Bmatrix}1,2,3,...,2024\end{Bmatrix}$   $escapes$  the pair  $(a,b)$  if for any elements  $s_1,s_2\in S$  we have  $\left|s_1-s_2\right| \notin \begin{Bmatrix}a,b\end{Bmatrix}$ . Let  $f(a,b)$  be the greatest possible number of elements of a set that escapes the pair  $(a,b)$ . Find the maximum and minimum values of  $f$ .
solution_md:
The minimum is  $675$  and the maximum is  $1344$ . The examples are  $(a,b)=(1,2)$   with  $x\in S\iff x\equiv1\pmod{3}$  and  $(a,b)=(674,675)$  with  $S={1,\dots,674,1350,\dots,2023}$ . For the minimum, notice that each number forbids at most to others, then there is a lower bound of  $1/3$ . For the maximum, consider the graph of  $2024$  vertices where there is an edge between  $x$  and  $y$  iff  $|x-y|=a~\text{or}~b$ .  $f(a,b)$  is the least number of vertices that need to be erased to remove all edges. Define the intervals  $I_2=[1;a+1[\cup]2024-a;2024]$ ,  $I_3=[a+1;b[\cup]2024-b;2024-a]$ ,  $I_4=[b;2024-b]$  where the numbers in it have degree  $2$ ,  $3$  and  $4$ , respectively. Clearly, the graph has a total of  $2a+3(b-a)+2(2024-2b)=4048-a-b$  edges. Let  $k=2024-|S|$  be the amount of numbers erased. There are three cases:
[list=1]
[*] $k\leq2024-2b$ : at most  $4k$  edges are erased, yielding  $4(2024-2b)\geq4k\geq4048-a-b\Rightarrow |S|\leq\frac{2}{3}\cdot2024-1$ [*] $2024-2b<k\leq2023-2a$ : at most  $4(2024-2b)+3(k-2024+2b)\geq4048-a-b$  edges are erased, giving again  $|S|\leq\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2024-1$ [*] $2023-2a<k$  at most  $4(2024-2b)+3(2b-2a-1)+2(k-2023+2a)\geq 4048-a-b$ , which simplifies to  $|S|<1012$ [/list]
PS: clearly the upper bound will be  $2/3$ , but the specific details of it depend of careful and boring manipulation of inequalities, here omitted.

stem_md:
We say that a triple of integers  $(x, y, z)$  is of *jenifer* type if  $x, y$ , and  $z$  are positive integers, with  $y \ge 2$ , and   $$ x^2 - 3y^2 = z^2 - 3. $$  a) Find a triple  $(x, y, z)$  of the jenifer type with  $x = 5$  and  $x = 7$ .
b) Show that for every  $x \ge 5$  and odd there are at least two distinct triples  $(x, y_1, z_1)$  and  $(x, y_2, z_2)$  of jenifer type.
c) Find some triple  $(x, y, z)$  of jenifer type  with  $x$  even.
solution_md:
**<u>*Part (a):*</u>**

At  $x=5$  we obtain  $\frac{28-z^2}{3} = y^2 \ge 4 \Rightarrow 16 \ge z^2 \Rightarrow 4 \ge z > 0$ , which we gives us the jenifer triplets: $\textcolor{red}{(x,y,z) = (5,t,1); (5,t,2); (5,t,3); (5,t,4)}$  for all  $t \in \mathbb{N}\backslash \{1\}$ .

At  $x=7$  we obtain  $\frac{52-z^2}{3} = y^2 \ge 4 \Rightarrow 40 \ge z^2 \Rightarrow 6 \ge z > 0$ , which we gives us the jenifer triplets: $\textcolor{red}{(x,y,z) = (7,k,1); (7,k,2); (7,k,3); (7,k,4); (7,k,5); (7,k,6)}$  for all  $k \in \mathbb{N}\backslash \{1\}$ .**<u>*Part (b):*</u>**

If  $x = 2n+3$  (for  $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ), then we obtain: $(2n+3)^2+ 3 = z^2+3y^2 \Rightarrow 4n^2+12n +12 =z^2 +3y^2$  (i).

Let  $z = n+A, y = n+B$  and substitution of these expressions into (i) gives us the system of equations: $4n^2+12n + 12 = (n+A)^2+3(n+B)^2 = 4n^2 + (2A+6B)n + (A^2+3B^2) \Rightarrow 2A+6B=12, A^2+3B^2=12$ ;

or  $(A,B) = (0,2);(3,1)$  (ii).  This in turns produces the jenifer triplets: $\textcolor{red}{(x,y,z) = (2n+3, n+2,n); (2n+3, n+1,n+3)}$  for all  $n \in \mathbb{N}$ .**<u>*Part (c):*</u>**

If  $x=2p, y=2q$  for some  $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ , then we obtain: $4p^2 -12q^2=z^2-3$  (iii);

of which the LHS of (iii) is even  $\Rightarrow z$  needs to be odd, or  $z=2r-1$  for  $r \in \mathbb{N}$ .  This leads to: $4p^2-12q^2 = 4r^2-4r-2 \Rightarrow 2p^2-6q^2 = 2r^2-2r-1$  (iv).

The LHS of (iv) is even, and the RHS is odd for all  $p,q,r \in \mathbb{N}$  (a contradiction).  


Now, if  $x=2p, y=2q+1$  for some  $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ , then we obtain: $4p^2 -12q^2-12q-3=z^2-3 \Rightarrow 4p^2-12q^2-12q=z^2$  (v);

of which the LHS of (v) is even  $\Rightarrow z$  needs to be even, or  $z=2r$  for  $r \in \mathbb{N}$ .  This leads to: $4p^2-12q^2-12q = 4r^2 \Rightarrow 0 =3q^2+3q +(r^2-p^2) \Rightarrow q = \frac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9-4(3)(r^2-p^2)}}{2(3)} = \frac{-3\pm \sqrt{9 - 12r^2+12p^2}}{6}$  (vi).

We require the discriminant in (vi) to be a perfect square, or  $3(3+4p^2-4r^2) =K^2 \Rightarrow 3+4p^2-4r^2 = 3^{2N-1}$  (vii) for  $N \in \mathbb{N}$ .  But (vii) has solutions in positive integers  $\Leftrightarrow p=r \Rightarrow q = 0, -1 \notin \mathbb{N}$  (a contradiction).

Thus, there are no jenifer triplets for even positive integers  $x$ .

Suppose that the line  $AP$  is perpendicular to the line  $OH$ . Prove that  $P$  belongs to the reflection of the line  $OH$  by the line  $BC$ .
solution_md:
Let  $(ABC)$  be the unit circle  $A=a$ ,  $B=b$ ,  $C=c$  and  $P=p$ . It´s well-know that  $H=a+b+c$  and  $N=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$ . 

Since  $N$  is the feet of perpendicular from  $O=0$  in  $AP$  which is a chord inscribed in the unit circle, we get that $N=\frac{a+b+c}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(a+p+O-ap\bar{O})=\frac{1}{2}(a+p) \Rightarrow p=b+c$  
Therefore,  $B+C=O+P$  so  $BCOP$  is a paralelogram so  $P$  is the reflection of  $O$  by the line  $BC$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $p$  and  $q$  be distinct odd primes. Show that  $$ \bigg\lceil \dfrac{p^q+q^p-pq+1}{pq} \bigg\rceil $$   is even.
solution_md: $$ \bigg\lceil \dfrac{p^q+q^p-pq+1}{pq} \bigg\rceil $$   =   $$ \bigg\lceil \dfrac{p^q+q^p-p-q-pq+p+q+1}{pq} \bigg\rceil $$   =   $$ \bigg\lceil \dfrac{p+q+1}{pq} \bigg\rceil $$   +   $$ \dfrac{p^q+q^p-p-q}{pq} $$     $$ -1 $$  =   $$  1-1+ $$   +   $$ \dfrac{p^q+q^p-p-q}{pq} $$  And since the numerator is even in the last fraction and the denominator is odd we are done.

A cricket wants to move across a  $2n \times 2n$  board that is entirely covered by dominoes, with no overlap. He jumps along the vertical lines of the board, always going from the midpoint of the vertical segment of a  $1 \times 1$  square to another midpoint of the vertical segment, according to the rules: $(i)$  When the domino is horizontal, the cricket jumps to the opposite vertical segment (such as from  $P_2$  to  $P_3$ ); $(ii)$  When the domino is vertical downwards in relation to its position, the cricket jumps diagonally downwards (such as from  $P_1$  to  $P_2$ ); $(iii)$  When the domino is vertically upwards relative to its position, the cricket jumps diagonally upwards (such as from  $P_3$  to  $P_4$ ).

The image illustrates a possible covering and path on the  $4 \times 4$  board.
Considering that the starting point is on the first vertical line and the finishing point is on the last vertical line, prove that, regardless of the covering of the board and the height at which the cricket starts its path, the path ends at the same initial height.

solution_md: $\textbf{EGMO T2 P4/2023 - Brazil}$ This is one of those problems that make me love combinatorics... ---------**Claim.** Let a vertical domino of type $i$ that vertical domino that occupies squares of rows $i$ and $i+1$ , and lif $a_i$ is the number of vertical dominoes of type $i$ , then $a_i$ is even $\forall i$ . *Proof:* Note that since horizontal dominoes fills an even number of squares in each row, it follows that $$ a_1+a_2 \equiv 0 \ (\text{mod} \ 2) $$ $$ a_2+a_3 \equiv 0 \ (\text{mod} \ 2) $$ $$ \vdots $$ $$ a_{2n-2}+a_{2n-1} \equiv 0 \ (\text{mod} \ 2) $$ Therefore, if some $a_i \equiv 1 \ (\text{mod} \ 2)$ , this must be true for all the other terms. But, noting that the number of dominoes need to be even, then $a_1+a_2+...+a_{2n-1} \equiv 0\ (\text{mod} \ 2)$ which does not happen if all the $a_i$ s are odd, therefore all are even. $\blacksquare$ ------- That said, defining for any walk $\mathcal{P}$ of the cricket in the board as $$ S(\mathcal{P})=\#\text{upwards movements in} \ \mathcal{P} \ - \ \#\text{downwards movements in} \ \mathcal{P} $$ We want to show that $S(\mathcal{P})$ is always $0$ . Thus, for any board filling, we will perform the following operations whenever we can [asy] size(8cm); void drawGrid(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; draw((x,y)--(x+2,y)--(x+2,y+2)--(x,y+2)--cycle, linewidth(1.2)); draw((x+1,y)--(x+1,y+2), linewidth(1.2)); draw((x,y+1)--(x+2,y+1), linewidth(1.2)); } void drawVerticalDominoes(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; pen p = red + 1.2; draw((x+0.25,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+1.9)--(x+0.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); draw((x+1.25,y+0.1)--(x+1.75,y+0.1)--(x+1.75,y+1.9)--(x+1.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); } void drawHorizontalDominoes(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; pen p = red + 1.2; draw((x+0.1,y+0.25)--(x+1.9,y+0.25)--(x+1.9,y+0.75)--(x+0.1,y+0.75)--cycle, p); draw((x+0.1,y+1.25)--(x+1.9,y+1.25)--(x+1.9,y+1.75)--(x+0.1,y+1.75)--cycle, p); } pair left = (0,0); pair right = (5,0); drawGrid(left); drawVerticalDominoes(left); drawGrid(right); drawHorizontalDominoes(right); draw((2.5,1)--(4.5,1), Arrow(TeXHead)); [/asy] [asy] size(12cm); pen p = red + 1.2; void drawGrid(pair origin, int cols) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; draw((x,y)--(x+cols,y)--(x+cols,y+2)--(x,y+2)--cycle, linewidth(1.2)); for (int i = 1; i < cols; ++i) draw((x+i,y)--(x+i,y+2), linewidth(1.2)); draw((x,y+1)--(x+cols,y+1), linewidth(1.2)); } pair left = (0,0); drawGrid(left, 7); draw((left.x+0.25,left.y+0.1)--(left.x+0.75,left.y+0.1)--(left.x+0.75,left.y+1.9)--(left.x+0.25,left.y+1.9)--cycle, p); draw((left.x+7.5,1)--(left.x+8.5,1), Arrow(TeXHead)); pair right = (left.x + 9, 0); drawGrid(right, 5); draw((right.x+0.1,right.y+0.25)--(right.x+1.9,right.y+0.25)--(right.x+1.9,right.y+0.75)--(right.x+0.1,right.y+0.75)--cycle, p); draw((right.x+0.1,right.y+1.25)--(right.x+1.9,right.y+1.25)--(right.x+1.9,right.y+1.75)--(right.x+0.1,right.y+1.75)--cycle, p); label("\ldots", (right.x+2.5,right.y+0.5), fontsize(16pt)); label("\ldots", (right.x+2.5,right.y+1.5), fontsize(16pt)); [/asy] Note that performing such operations never changes $S(\mathcal{P})$ . Now, I will show that given any filling of the board, performing the maximum number of operations of type $1$ and type $2$ always leads us to the generic board filled only with $1\times 2$ pieces where clearly $S(\mathcal{P})=0$ for every walk $\mathcal{P}$ . Suppose the square in the lower-left corner was covered by a $2\times 1$ . As $a_{2n-1}$ is even, by the claim, then there is another $2\times 1$ that covers a square from row $2n$ . Take the first $2\times 1$ with this property. Note that it must be at an even distance from the $2\times 1$ in the lower-left corner, otherwise we would have another $2\times 1$ before, which is absurd. Furthermore, we must therefore have the following pattern occurring [asy] size(8cm); void drawGrid(pair origin, int cols) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; draw((x,y)--(x+cols,y)--(x+cols,y+2)--(x,y+2)--cycle, linewidth(1.2)); for (int i = 1; i < cols; ++i) { draw((x+i,y)--(x+i,y+2), linewidth(1.2)); } draw((x,y+1)--(x+cols,y+1), linewidth(1.2)); } void drawDominoes(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; pen p = red + 1.2; draw((x+0.25,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+1.9)--(x+0.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); draw((x+1.1,y+0.25)--(x+2.9,y+0.25)--(x+2.9,y+0.75)--(x+1.1,y+0.75)--cycle, p); label("\ldots", (x+3.5,y+0.5), fontsize(16pt)); label("\ldots", (x+3.5,y+1.5), fontsize(16pt)); draw((x+4.1,y+0.25)--(x+5.9,y+0.25)--(x+5.9,y+0.75)--(x+4.1,y+0.75)--cycle, p); draw((x+6.25,y+0.1)--(x+6.75,y+0.1)--(x+6.75,y+1.9)--(x+6.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); } pair origin = (0,0); drawGrid(origin, 7); drawDominoes(origin); [/asy] However, since we operated to the maximum, in the regions over the $1\times 2$ , we will have sub-blocks like these because the number of $2\times 1$ that occupy this region is certainly even, and if there is no $2\times 1$ in this, we could have performed the type $2$ operation. Thus, at some point we will be forced to place [asy] size(2cm); void drawGrid(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; draw((x,y)--(x+2,y)--(x+2,y+2)--(x,y+2)--cycle, linewidth(1.2)); draw((x+1,y)--(x+1,y+2), linewidth(1.2)); draw((x,y+1)--(x+2,y+1), linewidth(1.2)); } void drawDominoes(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; pen p = red + 1.2; draw((x+0.25,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+1.9)--(x+0.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); draw((x+1.25,y+0.1)--(x+1.75,y+0.1)--(x+1.75,y+1.9)--(x+1.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); } pair origin = (0,0); drawGrid(origin); drawDominoes(origin); [/asy] or else, we would have to have [asy] size(6cm); void drawGrid(pair origin, int cols) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; draw((x,y)--(x+cols,y)--(x+cols,y+2)--(x,y+2)--cycle, linewidth(1.2)); for (int i = 1; i < cols; ++i) draw((x+i,y)--(x+i,y+2), linewidth(1.2)); draw((x,y+1)--(x+cols,y+1), linewidth(1.2)); } void drawDominoes(pair origin) { real x = origin.x; real y = origin.y; pen p = red + 1.2; draw((x+0.25,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+0.1)--(x+0.75,y+1.9)--(x+0.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); draw((x+1.1,y+0.25)--(x+2.9,y+0.25)--(x+2.9,y+0.75)--(x+1.1,y+0.75)--cycle, p); draw((x+1.1,y+1.25)--(x+2.9,y+1.25)--(x+2.9,y+1.75)--(x+1.1,y+1.75)--cycle, p); label("\ldots", (x+3.5,y+0.5), fontsize(16pt)); label("\ldots", (x+3.5,y+1.5), fontsize(16pt)); draw((x+4.1,y+0.25)--(x+5.9,y+0.25)--(x+5.9,y+0.75)--(x+4.1,y+0.75)--cycle, p); draw((x+4.1,y+1.25)--(x+5.9,y+1.25)--(x+5.9,y+1.75)--(x+4.1,y+1.75)--cycle, p); draw((x+6.25,y+0.1)--(x+6.75,y+0.1)--(x+6.75,y+1.9)--(x+6.25,y+1.9)--cycle, p); } pair origin = (0,0); drawGrid(origin, 7); drawDominoes(origin); [/asy] Which is absurd! Thus, we must have a $1\times 2$ covering the bottom-leftmost square. Repeating this argument inductively through the first row and then for the rest, we conclude that there are no $2\times 1$ pieces after maximum operations, $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md:
Decide whether there exists a positive real number \( a < 1 \) such that, for any positive real numbers \( x \) and \( y \), the inequality
\[
\frac{2xy^2}{x^2 + y^2} \leq (1 - a)x + ay
\]
holds true.
solution_md:
I claim there is no such  $a$ .

Suppose the contrary and write  $(1-a)x^3 + (1-a)xy^2 + ax^2y+ay^3\ge 2xy^2$ , namely,  $(1-a)x^3 + ax^2y+ay^3 \ge (1+a)xy^2$ . This is equivalent to
\[
x(x-y)(x+y)\ge a(x^2+y^2)(x-y).
\]
Suppose this inequality is valid for all  $y>x$ . Then,  $(1-a)x^2+xy<ay^2$  for all  $0<x<y$ , which implies  $x<ay$ . Now, take  $x$  such that  $ay<x<y$ , such  $x$  must exist as  $a<1$ , a clear contradiction.

candidates: Equivalent to  $(y-x)(ax^2 + ay^2 - x^2 - xy) \geq 0$ . For  $x=1$  and  $y>1$  we would like  $ay^2 - y + a - 1 \geq 0$  to hold for all  $y>1$  - but if it did, then taking the limit as  $y\to 1$  would imply  $2(a-1) \geq 0$ , i.e.  $a\geq 1$ , contradiction. Hence no such  $a<1$  exists.

Starting with Kellem and alternating turns, they add powers of \( m \) to the previous number on the board, such that the new value on the board does not exceed \( n \). Determine, for each pair \( (m, n) \), who has the winning strategy.**Note:** A power of \( m \) is a number of the form \( m^k \), where \( k \) is a non-negative integer.

stem_md: Let \( ABC \) be an acute scalene triangle with orthocenter \( H \), and consider \( M \) to be the midpoint of side \( BC \). Define \( P \neq A \) as the intersection point of the circle with diameter \( AH \) and the circumcircle of triangle \( ABC \), and let \( Q \) be the intersection of \( AP \) with \( BC \). Let \( G \neq M \) be the intersection of the circumcircle of triangle \( MPQ \) with the circumcircle of triangle \( AHM \). Show that \( G \) lies on the circle that passes through the feet of the altitudes of triangle \( ABC \).
solution_md:
Let  $K$  be the midpoint of  $AH$ . Since  $P$  is the  $A$ -queue point, it is known that  $P$ ,  $H$  and  $M$  are collinear. Therefore, define  $T$  such that  $HT\bot PM$  and also let  $L=KQ\cap N_9$  be the phantom point of  $G$ . We´re going prove that  $L \in (MPQ)$  and  $L \in (MHA)$ , thus,  $L=G$ . Initially, note that, by rotation,  $\angle PMQ=\angle AHT$ . Since  $Q$  belongs to the radical axis of both  $(APH)$  and  $N_9$ :  $QL\cdot QK=QP\cdot QA \Rightarrow PLKA$  is cyclic
Hence  $\angle PLQ=\angle PAK=\angle PAH=\angle AHT= \angle PMQ \Rightarrow L \in (PMQ)$  
However, since  $KM$  is the diameter of  $N_9$ ,  $\angle KLM=90$  and, from  $KA=KP$ ,  $\angle KAP= \angle KPA=\angle KLA$ Then,  $\angle ALM = \angle ALK + \angle KLM = \angle KAP + 90 = \angle AHT + 90 = \angle AHM \Rightarrow L \in (AHM)$  Q.E.D  $\blacksquare$

Since \( M \) belongs to \( (MPQ) \), \( (AHM) \), and the nine-point circle, we only need to prove that the centers of these three circles are collinear, as this would imply that they are coaxial and thus also intersect at \( G \).

Let \( D \) be the foot of the altitude relative to the side \( BC \), \( J \) the center of \( (AHM) \), \( L \) of \( (MPQ) \), \( N_9 \) of the nine-point circle, and \( K \) the midpoint of \( AH \).

Notice that \( \angle MPQ = 90^\circ \), because \( M \), \( H \), and \( P \) are collinear, therefore \( L \) is the midpoint of \( MQ \).

Also, observe that \( K \), \( M \), and \( D \) belong to the nine-point circle, but \( \angle MDK = 90^\circ \), therefore \( N_9 \) is the midpoint of \( MK \).

Thus, to prove that \( L \), \( N_9 \), and \( J \) are collinear, we will show that \( KJML \) is a parallelogram, whose diagonals intersect at the midpoint, solving the problem.

Let \( I \) be the circumcenter of triangle \( AMQ \). Note that \( H \) is the orthocenter of \( AMQ \), so \( J \) (the circumcenter of \( AHM \)) is the reflection of \( I \) across \( AM \), hence \( AIJM \) is a parallelogram. Moreover, it is a known property of the orthocenter that \( AKLI \) is a parallelogram (proven by the homothety centered at the centroid that maps the medial triangle to the original triangle, and the circumcenter to the orthocenter), thus we can conclude that \( KLMJ \) is also a parallelogram, completing the problem.

stem_md: The infinite sequence \( a_1, a_2, \ldots \) is defined by \( a_1 = 1 \) and, for each \( n \geq 1 \), the number \( a_{n+1} \) is the smallest positive integer greater than \( a_n \) that has the following property: for each \( k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \), the number \( a_{n+1} + a_k \) is not a perfect square. Prove that, for all \( n \), it holds that \( a_n \leq (n - 1)^2 + 1 \).
solution_md:
First terms of this sequence is  $1,2,4,6,9,11,13,15$ . Now suppose that  $a_k\leq (k-1)^2+1$  for  $k\leq N-1$  where  $N\geq 9$ . Let's prove that  $a_{N}\leq (N-1)^2+1$ . Consider  $S=\{(N-2)^2+2,...,(N-1)^2+1\}$  and  $A=\{a_1,...,a_{N-1}\}$ .  $S$  and  $A$  have no common element. Assume that  $a_N$  is not in  $S$ .  $|S|=2N-3$  and  $|A|=N-1$  hence there must exists some  $a_i$  such that both  $(N-2)^2+l+a_i$  and  $(N-2)^2+l+m+a_i$  are perfect squares for  $2\leq l<l+m\leq 2N-4$ .
\[\sqrt{(N-2)^2+l+m+a_i}\geq \sqrt{(N-2)^2+l+a_i}+1\]
\[(N-2)^2+l+m+a_i\geq (N-2)^2+l+a_i+1+2\sqrt{(N-2)^2+l+a_i}\]
\[2N-4>m\geq 1+2\sqrt{(N-2)^2+l+a_i}\geq 1+2(N-1)\geq 2N-1\]
Which is impossible as desired. $\blacksquare$

candidates: Let's use strong induction, base case is trivial. We wish to show $a_{n+1}\leq n^2+1$ . It comes down to a single lemma: **Lemma:** There is at most one $(n-1)^2+1 < q \leq n^2+1$ for wich $a_i+q =t^2$ , for each $i=1,2,\dots,n$ . **Proof:** If there were $q_1>q_2$ we would have: $q_1-q_2=t_1^2-t_2^2\geq (n+1)^2-n^2 = 2n+1$ . Because $q_1,q_2>(n-1)^2$ , but that's a contradiction because $q_1-q_2<(n^2+1)-((n-1)^2+1) = 2n-1$ . $_{\blacksquare}$ But because there are more than $n$ such $q's$ ( $2n-2$ to be precise) there must be at least one $q$ for which there is no $a_i$ with $a_i+q=t^2$ and that means $a_{n+1}\leq n^2+1$ , as we wanted. $_{\blacksquare}$

stem_md:
Let \( \mathbb{N} \) be the set of all positive integers. We say that a function \( f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \) is Georgian if \( f(1) = 1 \) and, for every positive integer \( n \), there exists a positive integer \( k \) such that
\[
f^{(k)}(n) = 1, \quad \text{where } f^{(k)} = f \circ f \cdots \circ f \quad \text{(applied } k \text{ times)}.
\]
If \( f \) is a Georgian function, we define, for each positive integer \( n \), \( \text{ord}(n) \) as the smallest positive integer \( m \) such that \( f^{(m)}(n) = 1 \). Determine all positive real numbers \( c \) for which there exists a Georgian function such that, for every positive integer \( n \geq 2024 \), it holds that \( \text{ord}(n) \geq cn - 1 \).
solution_md:
Cool problem. The answer is  $\boxed{c\le 1}$ , achieved by   $$ \begin{cases}n-1 & \text{if }n>1 1&\text{if }n=1\end{cases} $$   in which  $\text{ord}(n)=n-1$  for all integers  $n$ .

To see this is optimal, take the set  $X_k$  of integers  $x$  that satisfy  $\text{ord}(x)\le k$ , for a large integer  $k$ . The point is that  $X_k$  has atleast  $k+1$  elements, but each element of  $X_k$  is at most  $\frac{k+1}{c}$  by the condition if  $k$  is large enough. We thus get that for some  $k$ , the we have   $$ \frac{k+1}{c}\ge k+1 $$   so  $c\le 1$ , as desired.

stem_md:
Let \( n, k \geq 1 \). In a school, there are \( n \) students and \( k \) clubs. Each student participates in at least one of the clubs. One day, a school uniform was established, which could be either blue or red. Each student chose only one of these colors. Every day, the principal visited one of the clubs, forcing all the students in it to switch the colors of the uniforms they wore.

Assuming that the students are distributed in clubs in such a way that any initial choice of uniforms they make, after a certain number of days, it is possible to have at most one student with one of the colors. Show that 
\[
n \geq 2^{n-k-1} - 1.
\]
solution_md:
Consider the students as variables  $a_i\in\{0; 1\}$  depending on the color of their shirts.
One coloring will be represented as the  $n-$ tuple  $(a_1, a_2,\dots, a_n)$ .
Notice that if we can achieve a set  $A$  from  $B$ , the we can achieve  $B$  from  $A$ , just changing the same clubs.
Given a set  $S$ , we can change the clubs in  $2^k$  different ways, given that changing a club twice does nothing. Now, we know that, from any set  $S$  we can achieve a set  $T$  with at least  $n-1$  equal elements, thus for any set  $S$ , there is a set  $T$  with at least  $n-1$  equal elements from which we can achieve  $S$ .
A simple counting will tell us there are  $2n+2$  such sets  $T$ . Since we can operate  $2^k$  different ways in each  $T$ , the amout of  $T's$  times the amount of operations will give us at least the total amount of sets:  $(2n+2)\cdot2^k\geq 2^n\Rightarrow n\geq 2^{n-k-1}-1. 
 _{\blacksquare}$

stem_md: Consider 90 distinct positive integers. Show that there exist two of them whose least common multiple is greater than 2024.
solution_md:
Notice that  $\mathrm{lcm}(a,b)=\frac{ab}{\gcd(a,b)}$ . Also notice that by the Euclidean Algorithm,  $\gcd(a,b)\le b-a$ . Hence  $\mathrm{lcm}(a,b)\ge \frac{ab}{a-b}$ . If we require some least common multiple to be greater than  $2024$ , it is enough to find  $a$  and  $b$  such that  $\frac{ab}{a-b}>2024$ , or, equivalently,  $\frac{1}{b}-\frac{1}{a}<\frac{1}{2024}$ .

Let the numbers be  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{90}$  with  $a_1<a_2<\dots<a_{90}$ . We wish to show that for some  $i$ ,  $\frac{1}{a_i}-\frac{1}{a_{i+1}}<\frac{1}{2024}$ . Fix some  $t<90$ . Consider  $$ \sum_{j=t}^{90}\left(\frac{1}{a_j}-\frac{1}{a_{j+1}}\right)=\frac{1}{a_t}-\frac{1}{a_{90}}. $$  This implies by Pigeonhole that there is a gap of size at most  $$ \left(\frac{1}{a_t}-\frac{1}{a_{90}}\right)\frac{1}{90-t}. $$  Because  $a_t\ge t$  we get that this quantity is at most  $\frac{1}{t(90-t)}$ . Choosing  $t=45$  we get that the quantity is at most  $\frac{1}{2025}<\frac{1}{2024}$  and we're done.

So, the significance of the number  $90$  is that  $(90/2)^2>2024$  (just barely!)

stem_md: Show that if  $a < b$  are in the interval  $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$  then  $a - \sin a < b - \sin b$ . Is this true for  $a < b$  in the interval  $\left[\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ ?
solution_md: Let  $f(x)=x-\sin x$ . Then,  $f'(x)=1-\cos x$ . Note that  $f'(x)\ge 0$  for all  $x$ , so f(x) is a non-decreasing function. This means  $a - \sin a < b - \sin b$  is always true for  $a<b$ . Both intervals work.

stem_md: The remainder on dividing the polynomial  $p(x)$  by  $x^2 - (a+b)x + ab$  (where  $a \not = b$ ) is  $mx + n$ . Find the coefficients  $m, n$  in terms of  $a, b$ . Find  $m, n$  for the case  $p(x) = x^{200}$  divided by  $x^2 - x - 2$  and show that they are integral.
solution_md:
Let  $a(k)=x^k$ . I claim that   $$ m=\frac{1}{3}\left(2^k-(-1)^k\right) $$     $$ n=\frac{1}{3}\left(2^k+2(-1)^k\right) $$  We proceed by induction. The base case,  $k=2$ , gives  $m=1$ ,  $n=2$ , which is true.

Now, assume that   $$ a(k)=q(x)(x^2-x-2)+\frac{1}{3}(2^k-(-1)^k)x+\frac{1}{3}(2^k+2(-1)^k)=q(x)(x^2-x-2)+r(x) $$  Then,   $$ a(k+1)=(x\cdot q(x))(x^2-x-2)+x\cdot r(x) $$   so we simply need to find the remainder upon dividing  $\frac{1}{3}\left(2^k-(-1)^k\right)x^2+\left(\frac{1}{3}(2^k+2(-1)^k)\right)x$  by  $x^2-x-2$ .

To do this all we must do is multiply  $\frac{1}{3}(2^k-(-1)^k)$  by  $x^2-x-2$  and subtract it from  $x\cdot r(x)$ .

Thus, we have the remainder upon dividing  $a(k+1)$  by  $x^2-x-2$  is   $$ \frac{1}{3}(2^k-(-1)^k)x^2+\left(\frac{1}{3}(2^k+2(-1)^k)\right)x -\frac{1}{3}(2^k-(-1)^k)(x^2-x-2) $$    $$ =\frac{1}{3}\left(2^{k+1}-(-1)^{k+1}\right)x+\frac{1}{3}(2^{k+1}+2(-1)^{k+1}) $$  Which completes the inductive step. It's easy to see both terms are integers because  $2$  and  $-1$  are congruent modulo  $3$ The remainder for  $k=200$  is  $\frac{1}{3}\left(2^{200}-(-1)^{200}\right)x+\frac{1}{3}(2^{200}+2(-1)^{200})$

stem_md: Box  $A$  contains black balls and box  $B$  contains white balls. Take a certain number of balls from  $A$  and place them in  $B$ . Then take the same number of balls from  $B$  and place them in  $A$ . Is the number of white balls in  $A$  then greater, equal to, or less than the number of black balls in  $B$ ?
solution_md: Let  $X$  be the number of black balls in  $A$  and  $Y$  the number of white balls in  $B$ . Let  $q$  be the number of black balls taken from  $A$  to  $B$ . We then have to take  $q$  balls from box  $B$ , where  $q = p + b$ ,  $p\leq q$  ( $p$  and  $b$  are the number of black and white balls, respectively). If  $p = q$  then the number of balls in  $A$  is equal to the number of black balls in  $B$ . If  $0 < p < q$  then  $0 < q - p = b$ , which is the same number of black balls that will stay in  $B$ . And finally, if  $p = 0$  so  $q = b$ . So the answer is the same.

stem_md: Show that for any positive integer  $n > 2$  we can find  $n$  distinct positive integers such that the sum of their reciprocals is  $1$ .
solution_md:
It's clear that the integers   $$ 2, 3^1, 3^2, \ldots, 3^{n - 2}, 2 \cdot 3^{n - 2} $$   work for all  $n \ge 3$ , so we're done.  $\blacksquare$ **Remarks:** At first, I was thinking in terms of symmetric sums. Later on, I decided to consider induction. Unfortunately, inducting on  $n = a + b$ , where we assume the hypothesis for  $a$  and  $b$ , failed. Cauchy Induction didn't help either.

At this point, I realized we could prove the hypothesis for  $n = k + 1$  by *splitting up the smallest of the  $k$  reciprocals (for  $n = k$ ) into two fraction*s. Because   $$ \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = 1 $$   works for  $n = 3$  and   $$ \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} $$   I constructed a good sum for  $n = 4$  via the following process:   $$ 1 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \left(\frac{1}{2} \right) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \left(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} \right) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{18}. $$   The general case follows easily from here.

That is, we claim for all  $n\ge 3$ , there are  $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{N}$ , pairwise distinct, such that  $\textstyle \sum_{1\le i\le n}a_i^{-1}=1$ . To that end, for  $n=3$  it suffices to consider  $a_1=2,a_2=3$  and  $a_3=6$ , establishing the base case. Now, assume  $a_i$ ,  $1\le i\le n$  are such numbers. Note then that  $\textstyle\sum_{1\le i\le n}(2a_i)^{-1}+(1/2)=1$ . Clearly  $a_i>1$  for all  $i$ , thus the collection  $2a_1,2a_2,\dots,2a_n,2$  is indeed pairwise distinct sum of whose inverses is one due to the inductive hypothesis.

<details><summary>one-liner</summary>Since  $\sum_{i=k}^\infty \frac1{3^i} = \frac1{2\cdot 3^{k-1}},$  simply take  $\frac12+\frac13+\frac19+\cdots+\frac1{3^a}+\cdots+\frac1{3^{n-3}}+\frac1{3^{n-2}}+\frac1{2\cdot 3^{n-2}} = 1/2 + \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac1{3^i} = \frac12 + \frac12 = 1.$</details>

Induction on  $n$  works; for the base case of  $n=3$ , take  $\frac{1}{2}$ ,  $\frac{1}{3}$  and  $\frac{1}{6}$ ; for our inductive step, pick our first fraction as  $\frac{1}{2}$  and then split  $\frac{1}{2}$  into  $n$  reciprocals.

stem_md: Given  $5$  points of a sphere radius  $r$ , show that two of the points are a distance  $\le r \sqrt2$  apart.
solution_md:
Assuming all points lie on the surface of the sphere, and for any point  $P$  on the surface, define a  $P-$ *cupcake* as the surface of the hemisphere of radius  $r$  and centered at the sphere's center, which has  $P$  as its topmost point, including the boundary circle of radius  $r$ .
Note that if  $Q$  lies on a  $P-$ cupcake, then  $PQ\leq r\sqrt{2}$ . Then just note that you can't have more than three points on the surface of the sphere such that none of them lies in another's cupcake. In fact, when we have five such points, we have at least two pairs of points at a distance  $\leq r\sqrt{2}$  between them.
Edit: you can't actually ensure two pairs of points, but you can ensure at least one.

stem_md:
For which  $k$  does the system  $x^2 - y^2 = 0, (x-k)^2 + y^2 = 1$  have exactly:
(i) two, 
(ii) three real solutions?
solution_md:
The first relation is just  $y = \pm x$ , and the second relation is a circle centred at  $(k,0)$  with radius  $1$ . 

(a) Thus, the 2 solutions case is possible only if the circle is tangent to both lines, so  $k= \pm \sqrt{2}$ .

(b) Also, the 3 solution case is possible only if the circle passes through the origin, so  $k = \pm 1$ .

stem_md: A graph has  $100$  points. Given any four points, there is one joined to the other three. Show that one point must be joined to all  $99$  other points. What is the smallest number possible of such points (that are joined to all the others)?
solution_md:
This is a somewhat classic problem. I think you can prove this with relative ease by induction. You could also try fixing two vertices  $X, Y$  that aren't connected (which you can assume exist if the graph isn't complete), and considering quadruplets  $(X, Y, A, B)$  with  $A, B$  being variable vertices. <details><summary>Here's a solution via that.</summary>In all those quadruplets, we know for sure edge  $XY$  doesn't exist. So because of the 4-vertex condition, whether  $A$  or  $B$  is connected to the other three guys, edge  $AB$  for sure exists. Repeat for all pairs  $A, B$ ; letting  $S$  be the entire graph, we get that  $S/\{X, Y\}$  is complete.
Now call a vertex *cool* if it's connected to all other vertices, and consider all the previous quadruplets again. Take, for instance,  $(X, Y, A, B)$ . We know at least one of  $A, B$  is connected to both  $X$  and  $Y$ , and thus is cool. Then remove that vertex from  $S$  and repeat. We can do this until we have only three remaining vertices, meaning we removed  $n-3$  cool points from  $S$ ; hence we are done. The answer for  $n=100$  vertices is  $97$ .</details>

stem_md: Two thieves stole a container of  $8$  liters of wine. How can they divide it into two parts of  $4$  liters each if all they have is a  $3 $  liter container and a  $5$  liter container? Consider the general case of dividing  $m+n$  liters into two equal amounts, given a container of  $m$  liters and a container of  $n$  liters (where  $m$  and  $n$  are positive integers). Show that it is possible iff  $m+n$  is even and  $(m+n)/2$  is divisible by  $gcd(m,n)$ .
solution_md:
Let  $d = \gcd (m,n)$ ,  $\mathbb N$  is the set of positive integers,  $\mathbb N_0=\mathbb N \cup \{0\}$ . We have three containers: the largest,  $\mathcal L$ , having a capacity of  $m+n$  liters, that is initially full, and two smaller ones,  $\mathcal M$  of  $m$  liters and  $\mathcal N$  of  $n$  liters, that are initially empty. WLOG,  $m \ge n$ .
We can use only *precise* transfers, each one of which either empties or fills up one of two containers used in it. The volume of wine in each container is initially an integer divisible by  $d$ . It is not hard to see that a precise transfer cannot change this rule, since the number of liters transfered is either the full capacity of one of containers (when it is emptied) or the remaining space in it (when it is filled up). Thus, if  $(m+n)/2$  is either fractional or is not divisible by  $d$ , then it is impossible to obtain (exactly) such amount of wine in one of containers.
On the other hand, if  $(m+n)/2 = kd$ ,  $d \in \mathbb N$ , then it is possible to get  $kd$  liters in  $\mathcal M$ , leaving the same amount of wine in  $\mathcal L$ . Indeed, by Bezout's lemma, there exist  $a,b \in \mathbb N_0$  such that  $an-bm=kd$ . Let  $w$  denote the current amount of wine in  $\mathcal M$ . Apply the following sequence of steps  $a$  times:
[list=1]
[*]Fill up  $\mathcal N$  from  $\mathcal L$ . It is always possible since  $w \le m \implies m+n-w \ge n$ .
[*]If  $w+n \le m$ , transer all wine from  $\mathcal N$  to  $\mathcal M$ .  $w$  becomes  $w+n$ . Go to step 1 for the next iteration.
[*]If  $w+n>m$ , fill up  $\mathcal M$  from  $\mathcal N$ .  $m-w$  liters are transfered,  $n-m+w$  remain in  $\mathcal N$ .
[*]Empty  $\mathcal M$ , transfering all wine to  $\mathcal L$ .
[*]Transfer all wine remaining in  $\mathcal N$  to  $\mathcal M$ .  $w$  becomes  $w+n-m$ .
[/list]
It is easy to see that after  $i$  iterations,  $w=w_i=in-b_im$ , where  $b_i \in \mathbb N_0$ . Thus,  $w_a-kd=(an-b_am)-(an-bm)=(b-b_a)m$ . As  $w_a$  and  $kd$  are both in  $(0,m]$ ,  $w_a=kd$ .  $\blacksquare$ Note that  $(m+n)/2$  may be replaced by any other number  $h$  and the above reasoning may be used to prove the following fact: $h$  liters of wine can be obtained if and only if  $h$  is an integer between  $0$  and  $m+n$  that is divisible by  $\gcd (m,n)$ . Any amount from  $\{h, m+n-h\}$  that fits in  $\mathcal M$  (assuming  $m \ge n$ ) can go there, the other remains in  $\mathcal L$ ;  $\mathcal N$  is auxiliary only.

stem_md: $S$  is a  $(k+1) \times (k+1)$  array of lattice points. How many squares have their vertices in  $S$ ?
solution_md:
Throughout the solution, "square" means "square with vertices in  $S$ ". We call a square *crooked* if its sides are not parallel to the lines of the array, and we call it *straight* otherwise. Note that for every crooked square there exists a straight square that's circumscribed to it, that is, the vertices of the crooked square are contained within the sides of the straight square; note also that this straight square is unique. This means that if we count all of the straight squares along with all the crooked squares inscribed to them, we'll count each square exactly once.

Given a straight square  $ABCD$  with side  $n$ , we can choose an integer  $1\leq m\leq n-1$  and mark points  $P,Q,R,S$  in  $AB, BC, CD, DA$  such that  $AP=BQ=CR=DS=m$  to form a crooked square  $PQRS$ ; we can notice that those  $n-1$  possible values of  $m$  each correspond to a crooked square and that those are the only crooked squares inscribed in  $ABCD$ . We can also allow  $m=0$  to represent square  $ABCD$  in order to make calculations easier.

Now we proceed to count how many straight squares with side  $n$  there are. Since the lower-left vertex needs to be in the first  $k+1-n$  columns and in the last  $k+1-n$  rows, there are  $(k+1-n)^2 = (k+1)^2 - 2(k+1)n + n^2$  possibilities for the lower-left vertex and therefore  $(k+1)^2 - 2(k+1)n + n^2$  straight squares with side  $n$  in the array.

Thus, the number we want is:

[center] $\sum^{k+1}_{n=2} n \cdot [(k+1)^2-2(k+1)n+n^2] = \sum^{k+1}_{n=2} n(k+1)^2-2(k+1)n^2+n^3$ [/center]

Which, using  $1+\ldots+n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ ,  $1^2 + \ldots + n^2 = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$  and  $1^3 + \ldots + n^3 = \left( \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} \right)^2$ , eventually simplifies to:

[center] $\dfrac{k^4 + 16k^3 + 29k^2 + 14k}{12}$ [/center]

If I didn't mess up in my calculations.

stem_md:
Show that  $1 \le  n^{1/n} \le 2$  for all positive integers  $n$ . 
Find the smallest  $k$  such that  $1 \le n ^{1/n} \le k$  for all positive integers  $n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We see that  $n^{1/n}=\sqrt[3]3$  when  $n=3$ . Therefore,  $k\geq\sqrt[3]3$ .
Our claim is that the answer is  $k=\sqrt[3]3$ , that is,  $1\leq n^{1/n}\leq\sqrt[3]3$  for all positive integers  $n$ .

This is equivalent to showing that  $1\leq n\leq(\sqrt[3]3)^n$  for all positive integers  $n$ .
The left part of the inequality,  $1\leq n$ , is trivial. Now, we only need to show is that  $n\leq(\sqrt[3]3)^n$ .

It is easy to verify that this inequality is true for  $n=1,2,3$ . To prove that it is true for all  $n\geq4$ , we proceed by induction.
Suppose that it is true for  $n=k$ , where  $k\geq3$ . Then,
\begin{align*}
k&\leq(\sqrt[3]3)^k
\sqrt[3]3k&\leq(\sqrt[3]3)^{k+1}
k+1<\sqrt[3]3k&\leq(\sqrt[3]3)^{k+1}
\end{align*}

The last inequality is true, because  $(\sqrt[3]3-1)k\geq(\sqrt[3]3-1)\cdot3\approx1.3267...>1$ Hence, we have proven that  $1\leq n^{1/n}\leq\sqrt[3]3$  for all positive integers  $n$ .</details>

stem_md: Show that the maximum number of spheres of radius  $1$  that can be placed touching a fixed sphere of radius  $1$  so that no pair of spheres has an interior point in common is between  $12$  and  $14$ .
solution_md:
Let  $N$  be the maximum number of unit spheres that can all touch a fixed unit sphere in  $\mathbb{R}^3$  without overlapping. We show  $12\le N\le 14$ .

Lower bound ( $N\ge 12$ ). Place the fixed unit sphere at the origin. Take the 12 points
\[
(\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt2,0),\quad (\pm\sqrt2,0,\pm\sqrt2),\quad (0,\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt2).
\]
Each has norm  $2$ , so its unit sphere is tangent to the fixed one. For any two distinct listed points  $x,y$ , the vector  $x-y$  has at least two nonzero coordinates of magnitude  $\ge\sqrt2$ , so  $\|x-y\|^2\ge 2(\sqrt2)^2=4$ , hence  $\|x-y\|\ge 2$ . Thus  $N\ge 12$ .

Upper bound ( $N\le 14$ ). All centers lie on the sphere of radius  $2$ . If two centers subtend angle  $\psi$ , then their chord is  $4\sin(\psi/2)$ , so non-overlap ( $\ge 2$ ) gives  $\psi\ge 60^\circ$ . Place around each center a spherical cap of angular radius  $30^\circ$ ; interiors are disjoint. A cap on radius  $R$  with angular radius  $\alpha$  has area  $2\pi R^2(1-\cos\alpha)$ , so with  $R=2$ ,  $\alpha=30^\circ$ :
\[
A_{\text{cap}}=8\pi\Bigl(1-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr),\qquad A_{\text{sphere}}=16\pi.
\]
Hence
\[
N\cdot 8\pi\Bigl(1-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr)\le 16\pi
\ \Rightarrow\ 
N\le \frac{2}{1-\sqrt3/2}=8+4\sqrt3<15,
\]
so  $N\le 14$ . Therefore  $12\le N\le 14$ .

stem_md: Given  $n$  points in the plane, show that we can always find three which give an angle  $\le \pi / n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Kind of hard to explain, but I'll try.</summary>Let us have this one example. Consider these  $n$  points.

[asy]dot((0,0));
dot((1,2));
dot((3,3));
dot((4,-1));
dot((6,-3));
dot((5,2));
dot((0.5,-2));[/asy]

We place the  $n$  points on the Cartesian plane. Now, let  $P$  be the point with the least value of  $x$ -coordinate among all the  $n$  points. (If there are more than one of such points, then choose any one of the points.)

Therefore, all the rest of the  $n-1$  points must be to the right of  $P$ , or have the same  $x$ -coordinate as  $P$ .

[asy]draw((0,3.5)--(0,-3.5),gray);
dot((0,0));
label(" $P$ ",(0,0),W);
dot((1,2));
dot((3,3));
dot((4,-1));
dot((6,-3));
dot((5,2));
dot((0.5,-2));[/asy]

Next, draw a lines connecting each of these points to  $P$ .

This divides the right side of the Cartesian plane into... like...  $n-2$  angles.

[asy]draw((0,3.5)--(0,-3.5),gray);
dot((0,0));
label(" $P$ ",(0,0),W);
dot((1,2));draw((0,0)--(1,2));
dot((3,3));draw((0,0)--(3,3));
dot((4,-1));draw((0,0)--(4,-1));
dot((6,-3));draw((0,0)--(6,-3));
dot((5,2));draw((0,0)--(5,2));
dot((0.5,-2));draw((0,0)--(0.5,-2));[/asy]

Now, clockwise with respect to  $P$ , starting with the point with the highest slope with respect to  $P$ , name each point  $A_1,A_2,...,A_{n-1}$ .

It is clear that  $\angle A_1PA_{n-1}\leq\pi$ , because we defined  $A_1$  and  $A_{n-1}$  to be on the right side of  $P$ .

[asy]draw((0,3.5)--(0,-3.5),gray);
draw((0,0)--(1,2),red);label(" $A_1$ ",(1,2),N);dot((1,2));
dot((3,3));draw((0,0)--(3,3));label(" $A_2$ ",(3,3),NE);
dot((4,-1));draw((0,0)--(4,-1));label(" $A_4$ ",(4,-1),E);
draw((0,0)--(6,-3));label(" $A_5$ ",(6,-3),SE);dot((6,-3));
dot((5,2));draw((0,0)--(5,2));label(" $A_3$ ",(5,2),E);
dot((0.5,-2));draw((0,0)--(0.5,-2),red);label(" $A_6$ ",(0.5,-2),E);
dot((0,0));label(" $P$ ",(0,0),W);[/asy]

We have two cases.**Case I.**  $\angle A_1PA_{n-1}>\frac{\pi(n-2)}{n}$ .
The sum of the angles of any triangle is  $\pi$ . This implies that  $\angle PA_1A_{n-1}+\angle PA_{n-1}A_1<\frac{2\pi}{n}$ .
Hence, at least one of  $\angle PA_1A_{n-1}$  or  $\angle PA_{n-1}A_1$  must be less than  $\frac{\pi}{n}$ .**Case II.**  $\angle A_1PA_{n-1}\leq\frac{\pi(n-2)}{n}$ This implies that  $\angle A_1PA_2+\angle A_2PA_3+\cdots+\angle A_{n-2}PA_{n-1}\leq\frac{\pi(n-2)}{n}$ .
Hence, at least one of   $\angle A_1PA_2,\angle A_2PA_3,...,\angle A_{n-2}PA_{n-1}$  must be less than or equal to  $\frac{\pi}{n}$ .</details>

stem_md: $A, B$  are reals. Find a necessary and sufficient condition for  $Ax + B[x] = Ay + B[y]$  to have no solutions except  $x = y$ .
solution_md:
$A, B$ are reals. Find a necessary and sufficient condition for $Ax + B[x] = Ay + B[y]$ to have no solutions except $x = y$ .
Answer is $\boxed{|A+B|\ge|A|>0}$ Proof that this is necessary If $A=0$ then : $(x,y)=(0,\frac 12)$ is solution with $x\ne y$ If $A\ne 0$ and $|A+B|<|A|$ with $1>\frac{A+B}A\ge 0$ then : $(x,y)=(1,\frac{A+B}A)$ is solution with $x\ne y$ If $A\ne 0$ and $|A+B|<|A|$ with $-1<\frac{A+B}A\le 0$ then : $(x,y)=(-1,-\frac{A+B}A)$ is solution with $x\ne y$ Q.E.D. Proof that this is sufficient Let $n=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor x\rfloor\in\mathbb Z$ Equation is $y=x-n\frac BA$ Which may be written $\left\lfloor t-n\frac{A+B}A\right\rfloor=\lfloor t\rfloor$ where $t=x+n$ And it is trivial that $\left|\frac{A+B}A\right|\ge 1$ implies that only possible solution there is $n=0$ and so $x=y$ Q.E.D.

stem_md: A ball moves endlessly on a circular billiard table. When it hits the edge it is reflected. Show that if it passes through a point on the table three times, then it passes through it infinitely many times.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $AB$  and  $BC$  be two successive chords in the ball’s path. Let  $O$  be the centre of the circular table.
By the reflection law,  $\angle ABO = \angle OBC$ . 
Now  $\triangle OAB$  and  $\triangle OBC$  are isosceles. 
So  $\angle AOB = \angle BOC$ . Hence,  $AB =BC$ . 

Then every chord of the path has the same length (say  $d$ ). We now claim that through any given point  $P$  inside the circle there are at most two chords with length  $d$ . 
Let  $AB$  and  $CD$  be a chord containing  $P$ , with  $AP=a$  and  $CP=b$ . 
The power of  $P$  with respect to the circle is  $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$ , which is  $a(d-a) = b(d-b)$ . Hence,  $a=b$  or  $a+b=d$ . 
This means that  $P$  always divides the chord containing it in two segments of fixed lengths  $a$  and  $d-a$ . 
Now if three chords pass through  $P$ , the circle with centre  $P$  and radius  $a$  would cut the circle of the billiard table three times, a contradiction. 

Thus if the path passes through  $P$  more than twice, then on two occasions it must be moving along the same chord  $AB$ . 
That implies  $\angle AOB$  is a rational multiple of  $2 \pi$  and hence the path will traverse  $AB$  repeatedly.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Brazil Contests/Brazil National Olympiad/1986 Brazil National Olympiad/1680854.json

stem_md:
The Poincare plane is a half-plane bounded by a line  $R$ . The lines are taken to be 
(1) the half-lines perpendicular to  $R$ , and 
(2) the semicircles with center on  $R$ . 
Show that given any line  $L$  and any point  $P$  not on  $L$ , there are infinitely many lines through  $P$  which do not intersect  $L$ . Show that if  $ ABC$  is a triangle, then the sum of its angles lies in the interval  $(0, \pi)$ .
solution_md:
The Poincare plane is a half-plane bounded by a line $R$ . The lines are taken to be (1) the half-lines perpendicular to $R$ , and (2) the semicircles with center on $R$ . Show that given any line $L$ and any point $P$ not on $L$ , there are infinitely many lines through $P$ which do not intersect $L$ . Show that if $ ABC$ is a triangle, then the sum of its angles lies in the interval $(0, \pi)$ .
Poincare model of Lobachevskii geometry is well-known... Statement (1) is obvious. Statement (2) can be proved by the following construction. Consider Lobachevskii triangle $ABC$ and let $A'$ be the point symmetric to $A$ with respect to the absolute $R$ . Consider The inversion centered in point $A'$ . Then we get the Poincare model in circle (this circle is the image of $R$ ), where the traingle $ABC$ has vertex $A$ centered in the center of this circle. For such triangle statement (2) is obvious. As inversion is conformal transformation, statement (2) is also true for the first triangle $ABC$ .

stem_md: Find all primes which are sum of two primes and difference of two primes.
solution_md:
Since, all primes besides 2 are odd, and 2 is clearly not the sum of two primes, one of the two primes is 2.

Essentially, this means we need to find triplets of  $(p-2, p, p+2)$  where all three terms are prime. However, notice that the three terms are distinct modulo 3, so at least one of the terms is divisible by three. This means such triplets only exist if 3 is one of primes. It's easy to see the only such triplet is  $(3, 5, 7)$ , so our desired prime is 5.

stem_md: A figure on a computer screen shows  $n$  points on a sphere, no four coplanar. Some pairs of points are joined by segments. Each segment is colored red or blue. For each point there is a key that switches the colors of all segments with that point as endpoint. For every three points there is a sequence of key presses that makes the three segments between them red. Show that it is possible to make all the segments on the screen red. Find the smallest number of key presses that can turn all the segments red, starting from the worst case.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Consider any three points. Note that since it is possible to make all three segments red a monochromatic red triangle is achievable, thus we can conclude that the number of red segments is odd. Also, the parity of the number of blue segments of the triangle with these points as vertices doesn’t change while switching the keys. Then the number of blue segments in each triangle is even. 

Let  $P$  be one of the  $n$  points. Let  $A$  be the set of points connected to  $P$  by red points and  $B$  be the set of points connected to  $P$  by blue segments. 
Let  $A_1$ ,  $A_2 \in A$ . So  $PA_1$  and  $PA_2$  are both red and thus  $A_1A_2$  is red. 
Now consider  $B_1B_2 \in B$ . Then  $PB_1$  and  $PB_2$  are both blue and  $B_1B_2$  is red. 

Finally, consider  $A \in A$  and  $B \in B$ .  $PA$  is red and  $PB$  is blue, so  $AB$  is blue. Put  $P$  in  $A$ . This tells us that segments in the same set are red and segments connecting points in different sets are blue. Switching all points in set  $A$  will make all segments red. All segments in  $A$  will change twice, one time from each of its edges, all segments connecting points from  $A$  and  $B$  will change once, turning from blue to red and segments in  $B$  won’t change. This proves the first part.

For the second part, notice first that one needs to switch each point at most once. Let  $|A|=k$  and  $|B|=n-k$ . If we switch a point from  $A$  and  $b$  points from  $B$ , we change at most  $a(n-k)+bk$  blue segments. Suppose without loss of generality that  $k \leq n-k$ , hence  $k \leq \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor$ . Then  $k(n-k) \leq a(n-k) + bk \leq a(n-k) + b(n-k)$ , hence  $k \leq a+b$ . So the number of key presses is at most  $k$  and in the worst case,  $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor$ . 
This number is needed to make all segments red if  $|A|=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor$ .</details>

A function  $f$ , defined for the set of integers, is such that  $f(x)=x-10$  if  $x>100$  and  $f(x)=f(f(x+11))$  if  $x \leq 100$ .

Determine, justifying your answer, the set of all possible values for  $f$ .
solution_md:
A function $f$ , defined for the set of integers, is such that $f(x)=x-10$ if $x>100$ and $f(x)=f(f(x+11))$ if $x \leq 100$ . Determine, justifying your answer, the set of all possible values for $f$ .
If $x>100$ : $f(x)=x-10$ If $100\ge x\ge 90$ : $f(x)=f(f(x+11))=f(x+1)$ and so $f(x)=f(101)=91$ If $100-11\ge x\ge 90-11$ : $f(x)=f(f(x+11))=f(91)=91$ And a simple induction on $k$ proves that if $100-11k\ge x\ge 90-11k$ : $f(x)=91$ And so $\boxed{f(x)=\max(91,x-10)}$ and $\boxed{f(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\cap[91,+\infty)}$

stem_md:
Let $f(x)=\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$  $F_n(x)=f(f(f...f(x)...))$  (with  $n\ f's$ )

Suppose that  $f(0) \not =0$ ,  $f(f(0)) \not = 0$ , and for some  $n$  we have  $F_n(0)=0$ ,
show that  $F_n(x)=x$  (for any valid x).
solution_md:
Consider the equation  $f(x) = x$ , which gives the fixed points of  $f$ :
\begin{eqnarray*} f(x) = \frac{ax + b}{cx + d} &=& x  \Leftrightarrow \ ax + b &=& x(cx + d) = cx^2 + dx. \end{eqnarray*}

If  $c = 0$ , then  $f(x) = (ax + b)/d$ , a linear function, so every iterate  $F_n$  is also linear, and the above equation becomes
\[ ax + b = dx.  \]
Suppose  $a = d$ .  Then  $f(x) = x + b/a$ .  If  $b = 0$ , then  $f(0) = 0$ , contradiction, so  $b \neq 0$ .  But then  $F_n(x) = x + nb/a$ , so  $F_n(0) = nb/a$  can never be zero for  $n \ge 2$ , contradiction, so  $a \neq d$ .

That means the equation  $ax + b = dx$  has a solution; in other words,  $f$  has a fixed point, which means that  $F_n$  has a fixed point for all  $n$ .  We know this fixed point is not 0, since  $f(0) \neq 0$ .  But we also know that  $F_n(0) = 0$  for some  $n$ .  For this  $n$ ,  $F_n$  has at least two fixed points, and is linear, which means that  $F_n(x) = x$  for all  $x$ .

Now we can handle the case  $c \neq 0$ .  In this case, the above quadratic
\[ ax + b = cx^2 + dx  \]
has two roots (we can extend the domain of  $f$  to the complex numbers), so  $f$  has at least two fixed points.  We know that 0 is not one of these fixed points, since  $f(0) \neq 0$ .

Again as before, we know that  $F_n(0) = 0$  for some  $n$ .  For this  $n$ ,  $F_n$  has at least three fixed points, and by a straight-forward induction argument,
\[ F_n(x) = \frac{a_n x + b_n}{c_n x + d_n}  \]
for some constants  $a_n$ ,  $b_n$ ,  $c_n$ , and  $d_n$ .  Note that
\[ F_n(x) = x \ \Leftrightarrow \ a_n x + b_n = x(c_n x + d_n).  \]
But the quadratic can only be satisfied by three different values if and only if it is identically 0, i.e.  $c_n = b_n = 0$  and  $a_n = d_n$ .  Hence,  $F_n(x) = x$  for all  $x$ .

Note that the condition  $f(f(0)) \neq 0$  is not used anywhere.  This doesn't seem useful anyway, since you can check that  $f(f(0)) = 0$  if and only if  $b(a + d) = 0$ , and  $a + d = 0$  implies that  $F_2(x) = x$  for all  $x$ .

stem_md: Each face of a tetrahedron is a triangle with sides  $a, b,$ c and the tetrahedon has circumradius 1. Find  $a^2 + b^2 + c^2$ .
solution_md:
Inscribe the tetrahedron in a right parallelepiped which has edge of lengths  $ p,q,r$   we see that  $ a,b,c$   are the lengths of diagonals of each face of the parallelepiped. Since the circumsphere of the tetrahedron is the same sphere that circumscribed the parallelepiped,so it's enough to find the circumradius of the pararellepiped,which is half of its main diagonal. and the Pythagorean theorem gives  $ p^2 + q^2 = a^2$ ,       $ p^2 + r^2 = b^2$     and   $ q^2 + r^2 = c^2$ 
Since the half of the length of the main diagonal is  ${ \frac {\sqrt{p^2 + q^2 + r^2}}{2}}$ 

It follows that  ${ \frac {\sqrt{p^2 + q^2 + r^2}}{2}} = \sqrt {\frac {a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{8}} = 1$ 

Therefore,  $ a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 8$

**Lemma.** Denote $\delta_{d}(X)$ - the distance of the point $X$ to the line $d$ . Given are two lines $d_{1}$ , $d_{2}$ with the common point $A$ and a pozitive real number $k$ . Then the geometrical locus of the point $L$ for which $\frac{\delta_{d_{1}}(L)}{\delta_{d_{2}}(L)}=k$ is the reunion of two lines with its intersection in the point $A$ .**Proof of the proposed probem.** Suppose w.l.o.g. that $X\in AB\cap CD$ and $Y\in BC\cap AD\ .$ Denote the area $S=[ABCD]\ .$ $[APE]=BPE]=[CPG]=$ $DPG]=x\ ,\ [APY]=[DPH]=[CPF]=[BPF]=y\ ;\ x+y=\frac{1}{4}\cdot S\ .$ $[PAD]=[PBC]=2y$ $\Longrightarrow$ $\frac{\delta_{BC}(P)}{\delta_{AD}(P)}=\frac{AD}{BC}\ \mathrm{(constant)}\ ;\ [PAB]=[PCD]=2x$ $\Longrightarrow$ $\frac{\delta_{AB}(P)}{\delta_{CD}(P)}=\frac{CD}{AB}\ \mathrm{(constant)}\ .$ **Construction of the point** $P$ . Draw the points : $U\in (YC)\ ,\ YU=BC$ ; $V\in (YD)\ ,\ YV=AD$ ; $R\in (XA)\ ,\ XR=AB$ ; $S\in (XD)\ ,\ XS=CD\ .$ Construct the middlepoints $E$ , $F$ of the segments $[UV]$ , $[RS]$ respectively. Then the point $P$ is the intersection of the lines $YE$ and $XF\ .$

stem_md: There exists infinitely many positive integers such that  $a^3 + 1990b^3 = c^4$ .
solution_md:
Small generalisation:
For any integers  $a_1, \cdots, a_n, b_1, b_2 \cdots b_n, c$  such that  $\forall i, \gcd (a_i,c)=1$ , there are infinitely many solutions  $(x_1, x_2 \cdots, x_n, y)$  to \[ b_1x_1^{a_1} + b_2x_2^{a_2} + \cdots + b_nx_n^{a_n} = y^c \]

The key idea is to keep all the  $x_i$  as some powers of  $b_1 + b_2 \cdots + b_n$ . (Narrow down using CRT)

stem_md: The equation  $x^3+px+q=0$  has three distinct real roots. Show that  $p<0$
solution_md: Let the roots of  $x^3+px+q=0$  be  $a,b,c.$   Then, we have \begin{align*} a^3+pa+q=0b^3+pb+q=0c^3+pc+q=0.\end{align*}  Subtracting pairwise equations gives \begin{align*} (a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2+p)=0(b-c)(b^2+bc+c^2+p)=0(c-a)(c^2+ca+a^2+p)=0.\end{align*}  Since  $a\neq b\neq c$ , we have \begin{align*}a^2+ab+b^2+p=0b^2+bc+c^2+p=0c^2+ca+a^2+p=0.\end{align*}.  Adding them up gives   $$ (a^2+b^2+c^2)+(ab+bc+ca)+3p=0. $$    By Vieta's formulas,  $p=ab+bc+ca$  so we have   $$ a^2+b^2+c^2=-2p. $$    Since the sum of distinct squares is positive, then  $q<0.$   $\blacksquare$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Brazil Contests/Brazil National Olympiad/1992 Brazil National Olympiad/79804.json

candidates: typical method... first derivative,  $3x^2+p =0$ , must have two distinct real roots, which obviously implies  $p < 0$ .

Here is another method. Let  $a$ ,  $b$  and  $c$  be the roots of the equation, For  $a=b=c=0$  we obviously have  $p=0$ , so let's suppose that the roots are not all zero. Then we have, from Cardano-Viète relations:  $p=ab+bc+ca$  and  $a+b+c=0$ . From the last equation we get  $(a+b+c)^2=0$ , or  $a^2+b^2+c^2+2(ab+bc+ca)=0$ , or  $a^2+b^2+c^2=-2(ab+bc+ca)$ . The left hand side of this equation is strictly positive (it cannot be zero because  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  are not all zero); hence we have  $p=ab+bc+ca<0$  as desired.

stem_md: Show that there is a positive integer n such that the first 1992 digits of  $n^{1992}$  are 1.
solution_md:
This was posted with other numbers and the exponent instead of the base varying.
But more or less the same as for that works:

Let  $s = \underbrace{111...111}_{1992}$  and take  $t= \frac{\log_{10}(s) + \log_{10}(s+1)}{2}$  and  $\epsilon = \frac{\log_{10}(s+1) - \log_{10}(s)}{2}$ .
Now we are looking for an  $n$  such that there is a  $k$  with $10^k s \leq n^{1992} < 10^k (s+1)$ 
or equivalently $k + \log_{10}(s) \leq 1992 \cdot \log_{10}(n) < k + \log_{10}(s+1)$ 
or then sufficiently $|\log_{10}(n)-k-t| < \epsilon$ 

1. observation:  $\log_{10}(n)-t$  grows with  $n$  to  $\infty$ .
2. observation: the steps in which this term grows get as small as we want since  $\log_{10}(n+1)-\log_{10}(n) = \log_{10} \left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)$  which tends to  $0$  as  $n$  goes to  $\infty$ .

Thus when we take a big  $n$  such that the differences comming are all  $< 2 \epsilon$ , the sequence now can't miss the comming intervalls of type  $]k+t-\epsilon , k+t+\epsilon[$  and we get our integer of that type (one could now use this to explicitely a working  $n$ ).

stem_md:
Find all 4-tuples  $(a,b,c,n)$  of naturals such that
 $n^a + n^b = n^c$
solution_md:
After dividing through  $n^{\min(a,b,c)}$  we can assume that one of  $a,b,c$  is  $0$ , and it will for sure not be  $c$ , so WLOG  $a=0$ .
Then  $1+n^b = n^c$  is impossible when  $b,c >0$  since it gives  $1 \equiv 0 \mod n$  (and it's also wrong for  $n=1$ ).
Thus  $bc=0$ , and  $c=0$  is impossible as above, thus  $b=0$  and this yields  $2=n^c$ , having the only solutions  $n=2 , c=1$ , and this one works, giving that all solutions are of type  $2^k + 2^k = 2^{k+1}$ .

stem_md: In a chess tournament each player plays every other player once. A player gets 1 point for a win, 0.5 point for a draw and 0 for a loss. Both men and women played in the tournament and each player scored the same total of points against women as against men. Show that the total number of players must be a square.
solution_md:
Let  $k$  be the number of men and  $m$  the number of women, with  $n=k+m$ . The sum of the scores of man-against-man matches is  $\binom{k}{2}$ , so that is also the total points that men scored against women. Analogously, women score  $\binom{m}{2}$  in total against men. But  $km$  opposite-sex matches are played, so
\[ \binom{k}{2}+\binom{m}{2}=km  k^2-k+m^2-m=2km  (k-m)^2=k+m=n, \]
which is what we wanted to prove.

solution_md: [**This**](http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=16259) is similar but it asks only how many segments $DE$ are there [**Here**](http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?p=336213#336213) you can find a way to construct the segment, when $BC$ is the shortest side Simply $(ABC) = \frac{1}{2} AB \cdot AC \cdot sinA$ $(ADE) = \frac{1}{2} AD \cdot AE \cdot sinA$ $(ABC) = 2(ADE) \Rightarrow AB\cdot AC = 2 AD \cdot AE$ And the minimum length of $DE$ is when $AD=AE\Rightarrow AD^2 = \frac{AB\cdot AC}{2}$ So $AD$ is the geometric mean of $AB$ and $\frac{AC}{2}$

stem_md: Given positive real numbers  $x_1, x_2, \ldots , x_n$  find the polygon  $A_0A_1\ldots A_n$  with  $A_iA_{i+1} = x_{i+1}$  and which has greatest area.
solution_md:
Well, of course we need  $2x_i<x_1+x_2+\ldots +x_n$  for all  $i$  (otherwise no such polygon exists). In this case, there exist a polygon satisfying those condition and such that vertices  $A_0,A_1,\ldots, A_n$  are cocyclic. (My construction methods are a bit sloppy, but it should exists.)

Let's prove this polygon has maximal area. Glue on each side of our cyclic polygon an arc of the corresponding circle. Now move all side to get a generic polygon satisfying  $A_iA_{i+1}=x_i$ . Remembering the previous arcs, we get a "curvilinear polygon", with same perimeter as the original circle. Using the isoperimetric inequality, we know this curvilinear polygon has a smaller area than the original circle, and so our generic polygon has a smaller area than the cyclic one.

Remark : there might be some issues when arcs overlap each other, but I believe/hope this only happens in obviously non-optimal cases, like non-convex polygons.

stem_md: Find at least one function  $f: \mathbb R \rightarrow \mathbb R$  such that  $f(0)=0$  and  $f(2x+1) = 3f(x) + 5$  for any real  $x$ .
solution_md:
Indeed, we need  $ f: \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ . Consider the sequences given by  $ a_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} 2a_n \plus{} 1$  and  $ b_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} 3b_n \plus{} 5$  where  $ (a_0,b_0) \equal{} (0,0)$ . From the functional equation, it is clear that  $ f(a_n) \equal{} b_n$  for  $ n\in \mathbb{Z}^*$  satisfies the F.E. Furthermore, we can let  $ n\in\mathbb{R}\Leftrightarrow a_n\in( \minus{} 1,\infty)$ . We can find  $ a_n \equal{} 2^n \minus{} 1$  and  $ b_n \equal{} \frac {5}{2}\left(3^n \minus{} 1\right)$  so solving yields  $ f(x) \equal{} \frac {5}{2}\left((x \plus{} 1)^C \minus{} 1\right)$  where  $ C \equal{} \log_2 3$  which satisfies the F.E. for  $ x\in( \minus{} 1,\infty)$ . We WLOG set  $ f( \minus{} 1) \equal{} \minus{} 1$  and for  $ x < \minus{} 1$  we set  $ f( \minus{} 2) \equal{} 0$  and let  $ f(x) \equal{} f( \minus{} 2 \minus{} x)$  where  $ \minus{} 2 \minus{} x > \minus{} 1$ . This satisfies the F.E. as well:  $ 3f(x) \plus{} 5 \equal{} 3f( \minus{} 2 \minus{} x) \plus{} 5 \equal{} f(2( \minus{} 2 \minus{} x) \plus{} 1) \equal{} f( \minus{} 3 \minus{} 2x) \equal{} f(2x \plus{} 1)$  for  $ x < \minus{} 1$ . Thus, we have:
\[ f(x) \equal{} \begin{cases} \frac {5}{2}\left((x \plus{} 1)^C \minus{} 1\right) & \mbox{if }x\geq \minus{} 1 
\frac {5}{2}\left(( \minus{} x \minus{} 1)^C \minus{} 1\right) & \mbox{if }x < \minus{} 1 \end{cases}\mbox{ where }C \equal{} \log_2 3\]
And we can check that this works.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Brazil Contests/Brazil National Olympiad/1993 Brazil National Olympiad/79797.json

stem_md: The sequence  $(a_n)_{n \in\mathbb{N}}$  is defined by  $a_1 = 8, a_2 = 18, a_{n+2} = a_{n+1}a_{n}$ . Find all terms which are perfect squares.

\[\angle BAC = 30^\circ \]\[\angle CAD = 20^\circ\]\[\angle ABD = 50^\circ\]\[\angle DBC = 30^\circ\]

solution_md: By law of sines, $AP=2BP\sin50=\sin80 \cdot \frac{DP}{\sin20}$ Let  $\angle PCD=x$ , $CP=\frac{BP}{2\sin70}=\sin(80-x)\cdot\frac{DP}{\sin x}$ Dividing,   $$ \frac{AP}{CP}=4\sin50\sin70=\frac{\sin80\sin x}{\sin20\sin(80-x)} $$    $$ \implies \frac{\sin x}{\sin (80-x)}=\frac{ 2 \sin 20 \cos 20 \cdot 2 \cos 40}{\sin 80}=\frac{2 \sin 40 \cos 40}{\sin 80}=1 $$  Hence,  $x=80-x=40^{\circ} \implies PC=PD$ , as desired. $\square$

stem_md: Given a circle and its center  $O$ , a point  $A$  inside the circle and a distance  $h$ , construct a triangle  $BAC$  with  $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$ ,  $B$  and  $C$  on the circle and the altitude from  $A$  length  $h$ .
solution_md:
The circle is known, so let  $R$  be its radius and  $AD=h$  the altitude of  $\triangle ABC$ .

The triangle  $ABC$  is right so we have  $AD^2 = BD \cdot DC$  

But  $-BD \cdot DC$  is also the power of the point  $D$  with respect to the circle  $(O,R)$ 
 $-AD^2 = OD^2-R^2 \Rightarrow OD^2 = R^2-h^2$ 

 $\hline$ 

So, we construct the circles  $w_1 = (O, \sqrt{R^2-h^2})$  and  $w_2 = (A,h)$ .

If the two circles have common point(s), then take  $D\in w_1 \cap w_2$ .

The perpendicular line to  $AD$  intersects the circle  $(O,R)$  at the points  $BC$ .
 $\hline$ 

Now we should check if the constructed figure has the desired properties

From it's construction,  $AD$  is the altitude of the triangle  $ABC$ 
 $OD=\sqrt{R^2-AD^2} \Rightarrow OD^2 = R^2-AD^2 \Rightarrow -AD^2 = OD^2-R^2 \Rightarrow$  
the power of  $D$  w.r.t.  $(O,R)$  is  $-AD^2,$  but it is also  $-BD \cdot DC \Rightarrow$ 
 $AD^2=BD \cdot DC \Rightarrow \frac{BD}{AD} = \frac{AD}{DC} \Rightarrow$ 

The right triangles  $BDA,ADC$  are similar  $\Rightarrow \angle DBA = \angle DAC$ 
 $\angle BAC = \angle BAD + \angle DAC \Rightarrow$  $\angle BAC = \angle BAD + \angle DBA \Rightarrow$  $\angle BAC = 90^o$ 

 $\hline$ 

At first we should notice that  $h$  must be less than (or equal to)  $R$  because  $OD^2 = R^2-h^2$ 
(if  $h=R$  then  $BC$  is a diameter)

Also the circles  $w_1,w_2$  must have common point(s).

So we must have  $|OA-h|\leq OD\leq OA+h \Leftrightarrow$ 
 $|OA-h|\leq \sqrt{R^2-h^2}\leq OA+h$ 


If one of the equalities holds, then the circles  $w_1,w_2$  are touching, so we have one solution for  $D$ .

If  $|OA-h|< \sqrt{R^2-h^2} < OA+h$ , then the circles have two common points  $D,D'$  and we get two congruent triangles  $ABC$  and  $AB'C'$

stem_md: A real number with absolute value less than  $1$  is written in each cell of an  $n\times n$  array, so that the sum of the numbers in each  $2\times 2$  square is zero. Show that for odd  $n$  the sum of all the numbers is less than  $n$ .
solution_md:
induction. for  $n = 1$ , the result holds vacuously. assume it holds for  $n = k$  odd. in a  $(k + 2)\times (k + 2)$  such board, let  $B$  denote the sum of the squares on the boundary which aren't corner squares,  $C$  the sum of the corners, and  $I$  the sum of the interior. summing up the condition for all  $2 \times 2$  squares of the board, we get 
 $C+2B+4I = 0$ .

on the other hand, if we divide the board into a  $(k+1) \times (k+1)$  board (which can be broken up into  $2\times 2$  squares) and an L-shaped piece, the sum of all the squares on the original board, which we'll denote by  $S$ , is the sum of the squares in the L-shaped piece. this division can be done in 4 ways, and if we sum up the 4 results, we get 
 $3C+2B = 4N$ .

this equation and the one above give  $4N = 2C-4I$ , from which  $|S |= |\frac{C}{2}-I| \leq |\frac{C}{2}|+|I| < \frac42+k = k+2$ .

stem_md: We are given n objects of identical appearance, but different mass, and a balance which can be used to compare any two objects (but only one object can be placed in each pan at a time). How many times must we use the balance to find the heaviest object and the lightest object?
solution_md:
Here is the implicit argument that gives JBL's bound.

To prove that a given coin is not the maximum or minimum, we need to display a heavier and a lighter coin. Call a coin *light* if we've found a heavier coin and *heavy* if we've found a lighter coin. Our measure of progress will be the number of light coins plus the number of heavy coins. By the end of the algorithm, we should have a total of  $2n-2$ .

Imagine an adversary who controls the balance. If give him two coins about which we know nothing (neither heavy nor light), our progress must increase by  $2$ . Otherwise, he can make our progress increase by at most  $1$ . Thus, we can only get double progress on  $\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$  of our weighings. This implies a minimum number of  $2n-2-\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$  weighings.

Let  $a, b > 0$  be reals such that
\[ a^3=a+1 b^6=b+3a  \]

Show that  $a>b$
solution_md:
Let $ a > 0$ , $ b > 0$ be two real numbers such that $ \{\begin{array}{c}a^{3}= a+1 \ b^{6}= b+3a\end{array}$ . Show that $ a > b\ .$
**Proof.** Observe that $ a > 1$ and $ b > 1$ . Thus, $ \{\begin{array}{ccc}a^{3}= a+1 &\implies & a^{6}= (a+1)^{2} b^{6}= b+3a &\implies & b^{6}+a-b = 4a\end{array}\|$ $ \implies$ $ (a^{6}-b^{6})-(a-b) = (a-1)^{2}> 0$ $ \implies$ $ (a-b)(-1+\sum_{k = 0}^{5}a^{5-k}b^{k}) > 0$ $ \implies$ $ a > b$ because $ -1+\sum_{k = 0}^{5}a^{5-k}b^{k}> 5 > 0\ .$
**An easy extension.** Let $ \{m,n,p,r,s\}\subset [1,\infty )$ for which $ s\in N^{*}$ , $ p\le 2s$ and $ 4mn = p+r$ . Let $ x > 0$ , $ y > 0$ be two real numbers such that $ \{\begin{array}{c}x^{s}= mx+n \ y^{2s}= py+rx\end{array}$ . Prove that $ x\ge y$ .
**Proof.** Observe that $ x > 1$ and $ y > 1$ . Thus, $ \{\begin{array}{ccc}x^{s}= mx+n &\implies & x^{2s}= (mx+n)^{2} y^{2s}= py+rx &\implies & y^{2s}+p(x-y) = 4mnx\end{array}\|$ $ \implies$ $ (x^{2s}-y^{2s})-p(x-y) = (mx-n)^{2}\ge 0$ $ \implies$ $ (x-y)(-p+\sum_{k = 0}^{2s-1}x^{2s-1-k}y^{k})\ge 0$ $ \implies$ $ x\ge y$ because $ -p+\sum_{k = 0}^{2s-1}x^{2s-1-k}y^{k}> 0\ .$ **Remark.** For $ m = n = p = 1$ and $ r =s= 3$ obtain the nice proposed problem.
**A similar exercise.** Let $ a > 0$ , $ b > 0$ be two real numbers such that $ \{\begin{array}{c}a^{3}= 2a+1 \ b^{6}= 6b+2a\end{array}$ . Show that $ a > b\ .$

Given two such super-integers  $\ldots c_n \ldots c_2c_1$  and  $\ldots d_n \ldots d_2d_1$ , their product  $\ldots p_n \ldots p_2p_1$  is formed by taking  $p_n \ldots p_2p_1$  to be the last n digits of the product  $c_n \ldots c_2c_1$  and  $d_n \ldots d_2d_1$ . 
Can we find two non-zero super-integers with zero product?
 (a zero super-integer has all its digits zero)

This problem is probably from some older ISL or something like hat since it was used in a german TST some years ago.

We are looking for some solution to  $xy=0$  other than the trivial ones. Such solution exists, e.g.  $(0,1) \cdot (1,0) = (0,0)$  in the ring above.
So taking some  $x \equiv 1 \mod 5^n$  ,  $x \equiv 0 \mod 2^n$  and inversly  $y$  will give us the result, and they will fulfill all we want (they are unique determined  $\mod 10^n$ , thus by highering  $n$  the last digits will remain the same).

stem_md: Show that no one  $n$ -th root of a rational (for  $n$  a positive integer) can be a root of the polynomial  $x^5 - x^4 - 4x^3 + 4x^2 + 2$ .
solution_md:
We can try a generalization:

Let  $f ( X ) \in \mathbb{Q}[ X ]$  be an irreducible polynomial over  $\mathbb{Q}$ , of degree  $p > 3$  prime.
If  $f$  has precisely two non-real roots in the complex numbers, then no  $n$ -th root of a rational can be a root of  $f$ .

The overkill solution (as proposed by ZetaX) would follow from the following Galois theory fact
If  $f ( X ) \in \mathbb{Q}[ X ]$  is an irreducible polynomial over  $\mathbb{Q}$  and of degree  $p$  prime, and  $f$  has precisely two non-real roots in the complex numbers, then the Galois group of  $f$  is  $S_p$ .
Together with this classical group theory fact: If  $n > 4$ , then  $S_n$  is not solvable.
I believe this is enough motivation to start learning Galois :)

stem_md: $ABCD$  is a quadrilateral with a circumcircle centre  $O$  and an inscribed circle centre  $I$ . The diagonals intersect at  $S$ . Show that if two of  $O,I,S$   coincide, then it must be a square.
solution_md:
Case 1: Let  $O$  and  $S$  coincide at Point  $X$ .

Proof: Note that  $X$  is the circumcenter so  $XA=XB=XC=XD$  and let  $\angle XAB=\angle XBC=\angle XCD=\angle XDC=a$  and  $\angle XBC=\angle XCB=\angle XAD=\angle XDA=b.$   Since   $$ \angle A=a+b=\angle C, $$   then cyclic quadrilateral  $ABCD$  must have equal opposite angles, hence,  $\angle A=\angle C=90^{\circ}$ .  Similarly, we can get  $\angle B=\angle D=90^{\circ}$ .  Since the diagonals bisect each other, we have a square.  $\Box$ Case 2: Let  $O$  and  $I$  coincide at Point  $Y.$ Proof: Because  $Y$  is the circumcenter,  $\angle YAB=\angle YBA$  and   $\angle YBC=\angle YCB.$  But,  $Y$  is also the center of the inscribed circle, meaning that  $Y$  lies on the angle bisectors of angle  $A,B, C,D$ .  Hence,  $\angle YBA=\angle YBC,$   $\angle YAD=\angle YAB,$  and  $\angle YCB=\angle YCD.$  Hence,   $$ \angle DAY=\angle YAB=\angle YCB=\angle YCD $$   and  $ABCD$  is cyclic so  $\angle A$  and  $\angle C$  are both right angles.  Similarly,  $\angle B$  and  $\angle D$  are right angles.  Also,  $\angle DAY=\angle YAB=\angle YCB=\angle YCD=45^{\circ}$   so  $\angle AYB=\angle BYC=90^{\circ}$  so lines  $AYC$  and  $BYD$  are collinear and bisecting, which means that it is a square.  $\Box$ Case 3: Let  $I$  and  $S$  coincide at Point  $Z.$ Proof: In cyclic quadrilateral  $ABCD$ , we get  $\angle DAC=\angle DBC.$   But,  $\angle DAC=\angle CAB$  and  $\angle ABD=\angle CBD$  so   $$ \angle A=\angle B. $$   Hence,  $\angle A=\angle B=90^{\circ}$  and similarly, we can prove that  $\angle C=\angle D=90^{\circ}.$  Also, from equal base angles, we can prove that  $AZ=ZB=ZC=ZD$  so  $Z$  is also the circumcenter, proving that the diagonals bisect each other and it is a square.  $\Box$ Hence, given two of the three points coincide , we can prove that it is a square.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: $X$  has  $n$  elements.  $F$  is a family of subsets of  $X$  each with three elements, such that any two of the subsets have at most one element in common. Show that there is a subset of  $X$  with at least  $\sqrt{2n}$  members which does not contain any members of  $F$ .
solution_md:
Classical. Let  $Y \subset X$  be of maximal cardinality  $y$  so that it contains no member of  $F$ . Then for each element  $x \in X \setminus Y$  there must exist a member  $T_x \in F$  so that  $x\in T_x$  and  $|T_x \cap Y| = 2$ , otherwise we could augment  $Y$  by  $x$  and thus contradict its maximality.

But for any  $T_1,T_2 \in F$  with  $|T_1 \cap Y| = |T_2 \cap Y| = 2$ , it follows  $T_1 \cap Y \neq T_2 \cap Y$ , since any two members of  $F$  meet in at most one element. Therefore  $|X \setminus Y| = n - y \leq \binom {y} {2}$ , i.e.  $y^2 + y - 2n \geq 0$ , hence  $|Y| = y \geq \left \lceil \dfrac {-1 + \sqrt{1+8n}} {2} \right \rceil  \geq \left \lfloor \sqrt{2n} \right \rfloor$ .
